When consumed, capsaicinoids connect with pain receptors in the mouth and throat that are normally responsible for sensing heat. Once activated by the capsaicinoids, these receptors send a message to the brain that the person has consumed something hot. The brain responds to the burning sensation by raising the heart rate, increasing perspiration and releasing endorphins, called the body's "natural painkillers" and "happy hormones." Stomach . Chilies have long been associated with soothing the digestive system, by acting as stomach cleansers. According to the UK Food Guide, chili helps to settle stomach upset and encourages the production of good digestive acid. Chili aficionados believe the fruits can also induce weight loss because the substance that makes them "hot" speed up the body's metabolism. However, one study by the American Institute of Cancer Research performed in Mexico showed in 2003 that a high consumption of chilies (approximately nine to 25 jalapeno peppers per day) is in fact associated with stomach cancer. Immune system . Red chilies contain high amounts of carotene and vitamin C. It is said that chilies contain more vitamin C than citrus fruits. Chili peppers are also a good source of vitamin B6 and are very high in potassium, magnesium and iron, giving them a reputation for naturally boosting the body's immune system. Heart and other cardiovascular effects . A 2006 study published in the British Journal of Nutrition showed that after adding chili to the diet, bad cholesterol, that can often lead to heart problems, took a longer time to develop into heart diseases.

LONDON, England — Painfully hot, they make your eyes water, your heart race, and can turn your face embarrassingly red. Chilies have been used for many millennia for both their medicinal benefits and their exciting flavor. Once a staple only of cuisines from far-flung regions of the world, chilies can now be found in dishes across the globe.

Last week, an Indian woman wolfed down 51 “ghost chilies” — the world’s spiciest — in two minutes and smeared the seeds on her eyes in a bid to enter the Guinness World Records. Anandita Dutta Tamuly, 28, achieved the bizarre and fiery feat in the northeastern Indian state of Assam. She was cheered on by British chef Gordon Ramsay, who also attempted a bite of the scorching chili before begging for water.

A single seed can cause watering eyes, as well as a burning sensation in the mouth that can last up to five hours. A chili’s spiciness is measured in Scoville units: the number of times a chili extract must be diluted in water before it loses its heat. The “ghost chili,” also known as bhut jolokia, has more than 1 million Scoville units, while Tabasco sauce ranges from 2,500 to 5,000 Scoville units, and jalapeno peppers from 2,500 to 8,000 units.

Chilies have formed part of the diet in the Americas since approximately 7,500 BC and owe much of their fame to their sometimes unbearably spicy flavor. But they have also long been recognized for their health benefits. Scientific research — and legend — have attributed remarkable health properties to chilies over the years. Diego Alvarez Chanca, a physician on explorer Christopher Columbus’ second voyage to the West Indies in 1493, first wrote about the pepper’s medicinal effects in 1494.

Below, we look at the effects eating chilies has on the body.

**Skin**  
In addition to its flavor-enhancing qualities, chili is, oddly enough, used to fight the summer heat. Because chili causes extreme sweating and increased blood flow to the face, it cools the body when the sweat evaporates, making it useful for combating heat. These same heat-inducing properties are said to have a cumulative effect and, over time, are believed to alleviate pain when used in treatments for conditions ranging from arthritis and psoriasis to shingles and severe burns.

**Brain**  
The substances that give chili peppers their intensity when eaten or applied to the skin are called capsaicinoids. When consumed, capsaicinoids connect with pain receptors in the mouth and throat that are normally responsible for sensing heat. Once activated by the capsaicinoids, these receptors send a message to the brain that the person has consumed something hot. The brain responds to the burning sensation by raising the heart rate, increasing perspiration, and releasing endorphins, often called the body’s “natural painkillers” and “happy hormones.”

**Stomach**  
Chilies have long been associated with soothing the digestive system by acting as stomach cleansers. According to the UK Food Guide, chili helps settle stomach upset and encourages the production of good digestive acid. Chili aficionados believe the fruits can also induce weight loss because the substance that makes them “hot” speeds up the body’s metabolism. However, one study by the American Institute of Cancer Research conducted in Mexico in 2003 showed that high consumption of chilies — approximately nine to 25 jalapeno peppers per day — is in fact associated with stomach cancer.

**Immune system**  
Red chilies contain high amounts of carotene and vitamin C. It is said that chilies contain more vitamin C than citrus fruits. Chili peppers are also a good source of vitamin B6 and are very high in potassium, magnesium, and iron, giving them a reputation for naturally boosting the body’s immune system.

**Heart and other cardiovascular effects**  
A 2006 study published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* showed that, after chili was added to the diet, bad cholesterol, which can often lead to heart problems, took longer to develop into heart disease.

LONDON, England — Intensely fiery chilies can bring tears to your eyes, make your heart pound, and leave your face turning noticeably red. For thousands of years, they have been valued both for their supposed healing properties and for the dramatic flavor they add to food. Once mainly associated with the cooking of distant parts of the world, chilies are now used in dishes almost everywhere.

Last week, 28-year-old Anandita Dutta Tamuly of India ate 51 “ghost chilies” — regarded as the hottest chilies in the world — in just two minutes, and also rubbed their seeds into her eyes in an attempt to enter the Guinness World Records. The unusual and scorching feat took place in Assam, in northeastern India. British chef Gordon Ramsay was there to encourage her and tried a bite himself, but quickly asked for water.

Even a single seed from a ghost chili can make the eyes water and create a burning feeling in the mouth that may continue for as long as five hours. The heat of a chili is rated using Scoville units, which indicate how many times chili extract must be diluted with water before its burning quality disappears. The ghost chili, or bhut jolokia, measures more than 1 million Scoville units. By comparison, Tabasco sauce falls between 2,500 and 5,000 Scoville units, while jalapeno peppers range from 2,500 to 8,000.

Chilies have been eaten in the Americas since around 7,500 BC. They are best known for their sometimes overwhelmingly hot taste, but they have also been credited for centuries with health-related benefits. Over time, both scientific studies and traditional beliefs have linked chilies with remarkable effects on the body. Diego Alvarez Chanca, a doctor who traveled with Christopher Columbus on his second expedition to the West Indies in 1493, was the first to write about the pepper’s medicinal properties in 1494.

Here are some of the ways chili consumption affects the body.

**Skin**  
Although chilies are famous for improving the taste of food, they are also, somewhat surprisingly, used to help cope with summer heat. Because eating chili can cause heavy sweating and bring blood to the face, the body may cool down as the sweat evaporates. These heat-producing effects are also believed to build up over time, and they are said to help reduce pain when used in treatments for conditions ranging from arthritis and psoriasis to shingles and serious burns.

**Brain**  
The compounds responsible for the sharp heat of chili peppers, whether eaten or placed on the skin, are known as capsaicinoids. When they are consumed, capsaicinoids attach to pain receptors in the mouth and throat, the same receptors that normally detect heat. Once stimulated, these receptors signal to the brain that something hot has been eaten. In response to the burning feeling, the brain increases the heart rate, triggers sweating, and releases endorphins — chemicals often described as the body’s natural painkillers and “happy hormones.”

**Stomach**  
Chilies have traditionally been linked with calming digestion and are thought to act as cleansers for the stomach. The UK Food Guide says chili can help ease an upset stomach and promote the production of beneficial digestive acid. Fans of chili also argue that the fruits may support weight loss because the compound responsible for their heat can raise the body’s metabolism. However, a 2003 study carried out in Mexico by the American Institute of Cancer Research found that eating large quantities of chilies — roughly nine to 25 jalapeno peppers a day — was actually associated with stomach cancer.

**Immune system**  
Red chilies are rich in carotene and vitamin C, and it is often said that they contain more vitamin C than citrus fruits. They are also a good source of vitamin B6 and contain very high levels of potassium, magnesium, and iron. Because of this, they have gained a reputation as a natural way to strengthen the immune system.

**Heart and cardiovascular effects**  
Research published in the *British Journal of Nutrition* in 2006 found that when chili was added to the diet, “bad” cholesterol — which can contribute to heart problems — took longer to develop into heart disease.

Chilies have long held a special place in cuisines, cultures, and medical traditions around the world. They are eaten for pleasure, used to add heat and depth to food, celebrated in contests, and studied by scientists for their remarkable effects on the human body. Among the many varieties of chili peppers, one of the most famous is the ultra-hot “ghost chili,” also known as *bhut jolokia*. Native to parts of northeastern India, this pepper became internationally known because of its extraordinary heat and the dramatic reactions it can produce in those brave enough to eat it.

One striking example of the ghost chili’s cultural importance is the record attempt by Anandita Dutta Tamuly of Assam, India. She became known for her astonishing ability to consume extremely hot chilies and even rub them on her eyes without appearing to suffer the kind of distress most people would expect. Her performance drew global attention not only because it seemed almost unbelievable, but also because it demonstrated the deep familiarity that some communities have with chilies as part of everyday life. In regions where very hot peppers are commonly grown and eaten, tolerance can be built over time, and chilies may be treated not as exotic curiosities but as ordinary and valued ingredients.

The intensity of chili peppers is commonly measured using Scoville heat units, a scale developed to estimate the concentration of capsaicin, the chemical compound chiefly responsible for their burning sensation. Mild peppers register low on the scale, while very hot peppers can reach hundreds of thousands or even more than a million Scoville units. The ghost chili gained fame because it was once recognized as one of the hottest peppers in the world, measuring over one million Scoville units in some tests. Such numbers help explain why eating these peppers can cause sweating, tearing, a runny nose, hiccups, and a powerful burning feeling in the mouth and throat.

Scientifically, the heat of chilies is unusual because it is not a “taste” in the ordinary sense. Capsaicin activates pain and heat receptors in the body, especially receptors known as TRPV1, which normally respond to high temperatures. When capsaicin binds to these receptors, the brain interprets the signal as burning heat, even though no actual burn is taking place. This is why a person eating a hot chili may feel as if their mouth is on fire. The body then reacts with defensive responses: increased saliva, sweating to cool the body, and the release of endorphins, which can create a sense of excitement or even pleasure after the initial pain.

Historically, chilies have traveled far beyond their original home in the Americas. After European contact with the New World, chili peppers spread quickly through trade routes to Asia, Africa, and Europe. They were readily adopted into local cuisines because they were easy to grow, intensely flavorful, and useful in preserving or enlivening food. Today, it is difficult to imagine Indian, Thai, Korean, Mexican, Ethiopian, or many other culinary traditions without chili peppers. Their global journey shows how a single plant can transform eating habits across continents.

Chilies have also been valued for their medicinal qualities. In traditional systems of healing, they have been used to stimulate digestion, improve circulation, relieve congestion, and warm the body. Modern science has found that capsaicin can have practical medical uses as well. It is used in creams and patches to help relieve certain kinds of pain, including nerve pain and muscle aches. By repeatedly stimulating pain receptors, capsaicin can eventually reduce their sensitivity, making it useful in controlled therapeutic settings. Researchers have also studied chilies for possible effects on metabolism, appetite, inflammation, and cardiovascular health, though such benefits depend on amount, context, and individual tolerance.

At the same time, the power of chilies should not be underestimated. Extremely hot peppers can cause intense discomfort, nausea, stomach pain, or other adverse reactions, especially when consumed in large quantities or by people unaccustomed to them. Chili-eating contests and record attempts often turn the pepper into a spectacle, but they also reveal the limits of the human body. What is thrilling for one person may be overwhelming or dangerous for another. This tension between pleasure and pain is part of what makes chilies so fascinating.

Ultimately, chilies are valued for much more than their heat. They bring flavor, color, excitement, and identity to food. They inspire festivals, competitions, scientific research, and medical applications. The ghost chili, with its fierce reputation and cultural roots, represents the extreme end of a much broader human relationship with spicy plants. Whether used in a home-cooked meal, tested in a laboratory, or displayed in a daring public performance, chilies continue to show their importance as both cultural symbols and agents of physical sensation. Their enduring appeal lies in the way they connect taste, pain, health, tradition, and spectacle across the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style health article from London about chilies, opening with Anandita Dutta Tamuly eating 51 ghost chilies for a Guinness World Record, then explaining Scoville units and the effects of chilies on the skin, brain, stomach, immune system, and heart.

**London —** Anandita Dutta Tamuly sat before a plate of one of the world’s most fearsome foods and began to eat. One after another, she consumed 51 ghost chilies — the blistering Indian pepper also known as *bhut jolokia* — in a Guinness World Record attempt that turned her tolerance for heat into global spectacle.

For most people, even one ghost chili would be overwhelming. The pepper can measure around **1 million Scoville Heat Units**, a rating that places it far above a jalapeño and into the category of foods capable of causing tears, sweating, coughing and intense burning sensations.

But why do chilies feel hot — and what do they actually do to the body?

## What are Scoville units?

The “heat” in chili peppers comes mainly from **capsaicin**, a chemical compound concentrated in the pepper’s white inner membrane and, to a lesser extent, its seeds.

Chili strength is commonly measured using the **Scoville scale**, named after American pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, who developed an early taste-based test in 1912. Today, labs more often use chemical analysis to estimate capsaicinoid content, but the results are still commonly expressed in Scoville Heat Units, or SHU.

A rough guide:

- **Bell pepper:** 0 SHU  
- **Jalapeño:** about 2,500–8,000 SHU  
- **Cayenne pepper:** about 30,000–50,000 SHU  
- **Habanero:** about 100,000–350,000 SHU  
- **Ghost chili:** around 800,000–1,000,000+ SHU  
- **Pepper spray:** often several million SHU  

The higher the number, the more capsaicin-like compounds are present — and the more intense the burning sensation.

## Why chilies burn your skin and mouth

Capsaicin does not actually burn tissue the way heat or acid does. Instead, it binds to pain receptors called **TRPV1 receptors**, which help the body detect high temperature and physical irritation.

When capsaicin activates these receptors, the brain interprets the signal as burning heat. That is why chili can make your mouth feel as though it is on fire even when the pepper is at room temperature.

On the skin, capsaicin can cause:

- Redness  
- Tingling or burning  
- Irritation  
- Sweating  
- Temporary numbness after repeated exposure  

This is also why people are advised to wear gloves when handling very hot peppers. Touching the eyes, nose or genitals after cutting chilies can cause severe discomfort.

Interestingly, capsaicin is also used medicinally in some creams and patches for nerve pain and arthritis. Repeated low-dose exposure can desensitize pain nerves over time — though that is very different from casually rubbing a superhot chili on the skin.

## What chilies do to the brain

The pain signal from chili peppers can trigger a cascade in the nervous system. For some people, eating spicy food leads to an intense but enjoyable rush.

That happens partly because the brain responds to perceived pain by releasing chemicals such as **endorphins** and **dopamine**, which can produce feelings of pleasure, relief or even euphoria.

This may explain why some chili lovers chase hotter and hotter peppers. The experience combines pain, thrill and reward — a kind of culinary roller coaster.

However, the brain does not interpret extreme chili exposure lightly. Very hot peppers can cause watery eyes, panic-like sensations, sweating, rapid breathing and a strong urge to stop eating. In rare cases, extreme reactions have been linked to severe headaches or spikes in blood pressure, especially in people with underlying health risks.

## The stomach: irritation, not usually damage

A common myth is that spicy food “burns holes” in the stomach. For most healthy people, that is not true. The stomach is built to handle acid and irritation, and moderate chili intake does not usually cause ulcers.

In fact, stomach ulcers are most commonly linked to **Helicobacter pylori** infection or long-term use of certain painkillers such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Still, chilies can aggravate symptoms in some people. Capsaicin may worsen:

- Heartburn or acid reflux  
- Indigestion  
- Irritable bowel symptoms  
- Nausea  
- Diarrhea  
- Abdominal cramping  

Very large amounts of extremely hot chilies can cause vomiting, intense abdominal pain and dehydration. People with reflux disease, inflammatory bowel disease or sensitive digestive systems may need to limit very spicy foods.

## Chilies and the immune system

Chilies are more than just capsaicin. Many varieties contain nutrients such as:

- **Vitamin C**  
- **Vitamin A precursors**, including carotenoids  
- **Vitamin B6**  
- **Potassium**  
- Antioxidant plant compounds  

Vitamin C supports normal immune function, and antioxidants help protect cells from oxidative stress. But chilies are not a cure for infections, and eating spicy food will not “boost” immunity in a dramatic or immediate way.

There is also some laboratory evidence that capsaicin has anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties, but effects seen in cells or animals do not always translate into clear health benefits in humans.

In short: chilies can be part of a healthy diet, but they are not a medical treatment.

## What about the heart?

Research on chili consumption and heart health has produced intriguing findings. Some observational studies have linked regular chili intake with lower rates of death from cardiovascular disease. Possible explanations include effects on metabolism, inflammation, blood vessel function and cholesterol levels.

But these studies cannot prove that chilies alone protect the heart. People who eat chilies may also have different diets, lifestyles or cultural eating patterns that influence health outcomes.

Capsaicin may temporarily increase heart rate, body temperature and sweating. For most healthy adults, that response is harmless. But people with heart rhythm problems, uncontrolled high blood pressure or a history of cardiovascular events should be cautious with extreme chili challenges.

Eating a spicy curry is one thing. Eating dozens of ghost peppers is another.

## Can chilies be dangerous?

For most people, normal culinary use of chilies is safe. The risks rise with superhot peppers, extracts and eating contests.

Possible problems include:

- Severe mouth and throat pain  
- Vomiting  
- Breathing difficulty from coughing or throat irritation  
- Eye injury from accidental contact  
- Severe stomach pain  
- Dehydration  
- Rare but serious reactions such as intense headaches or cardiovascular stress  

Milk, yogurt and other dairy products may help ease the burn because capsaicin dissolves better in fat than in water. Drinking water alone often spreads the sensation rather than stopping it.

## The bottom line

Chilies trick the nervous system into feeling heat, setting off reactions in the skin, brain, gut and cardiovascular system. In moderate amounts, they can add flavor, nutrients and enjoyment to meals. For chili enthusiasts, they may even provide a rush.

But the kind of feat performed by Anandita Dutta Tamuly is not a model for everyday eating. Superhot chilies can push the body hard, and extreme challenges carry real risks.

For most people, the healthiest approach is simple: enjoy the heat — but respect it.

# Fire in the Fruit: What Chili Peppers Do to the Body — and Why Medicine Is Paying Attention

When a chili pepper bites back, the sensation can feel like injury: lips sting, eyes water, sweat beads, the nose runs, and the stomach may protest. But the “burn” is not heat in the ordinary sense. It is chemistry — mainly the work of capsaicin and related compounds called capsaicinoids — tricking the nervous system into sounding a fire alarm.

That alarm has made chilies objects of fascination not only in kitchens, but also in laboratories and clinics. From mild jalapeños to the fearsome ghost chili, or *bhut jolokia*, peppers have been studied for pain relief, metabolism, cardiovascular effects, digestion, inflammation, and even antimicrobial activity. Their benefits, however, come with limits: the same compounds that may help control pain or stimulate circulation can also irritate the gut, trigger reflux, or cause intense distress when consumed in extreme quantities.

Few peppers symbolize that double edge better than the ghost chili.

## The Ghost Chili: A Pepper With a Reputation

The ghost chili — known in India as *bhut jolokia* and associated especially with Assam, Nagaland, and other parts of northeastern India — was once widely cited as one of the world’s hottest peppers. It can exceed 1 million Scoville Heat Units, far surpassing common hot peppers such as jalapeños, which usually range from about 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units.

Its heat made it a global spectacle. In 2009, British chef Gordon Ramsay witnessed an extraordinary record attempt in India by Anandita Dutta Tamuly, an Assamese woman known for her tolerance of hot peppers. During the event, she reportedly ate dozens of ghost chilies in a matter of minutes and rubbed the peppers near her eyes — a feat that stunned observers and helped introduce many international viewers to the sheer intensity of *bhut jolokia*.

Such demonstrations are not medical recommendations. Extreme chili-eating can cause vomiting, severe abdominal pain, faintness, spikes in stress hormones, and, in rare cases, serious complications. But the spectacle highlights a scientific question: why can one plant produce such powerful effects on the human body?

## The Chemistry of the Burn

Capsaicin binds to a receptor in the body called TRPV1, found on sensory nerves. TRPV1 normally responds to high heat, abrasion, and acidity. When capsaicin activates it, the brain receives a message that the tissue is burning — even though no actual thermal burn has occurred.

This is why chilies feel hot, why milk soothes better than water, and why repeated exposure can change the experience. Capsaicin is fat-soluble, so dairy fat can help lift it from the mouth. Water often spreads it around. Over time, repeated stimulation can temporarily desensitize pain fibers, which is one reason capsaicin has medical uses.

# How Chilies Affect the Body

## 1. Mouth and Throat: The First Alarm

The mouth is where capsaicin first meets nerve endings. The immediate effects include:

- Burning or stinging pain  
- Increased saliva  
- Tingling or numbness  
- Coughing or throat irritation  
- Runny nose and watery eyes  

This response is protective. The body interprets capsaicin as a threat and tries to flush it away with saliva, tears, and mucus.

Medicinally, this intense nerve activation is important. Repeated capsaicin exposure can reduce the sensitivity of certain pain pathways. That principle is used in capsaicin creams and patches for some chronic pain conditions.

## 2. Nose, Eyes, and Sinuses: Tears, Mucus, and Irritation

Chili fumes or direct contact can irritate mucous membranes. That is why chopping hot peppers and then touching the eyes can be so painful. Capsaicin can trigger:

- Tearing  
- Sneezing  
- Nasal drainage  
- Burning around the eyes  
- Temporary swelling or redness  

Some people feel that spicy food “clears the sinuses.” In reality, capsaicin stimulates nasal secretions and can temporarily make the nose run, which may create a sensation of relief. It does not cure infections, but it may briefly ease congestion for some people.

## 3. Brain and Nervous System: Pain, Pleasure, and Endorphins

The brain receives capsaicin’s signal as pain. In response, it may release endorphins and other neurochemicals associated with relief or pleasure. This helps explain why many people enjoy intensely spicy food despite the discomfort.

Potential nervous-system effects include:

- A rush or “high” after eating spicy food  
- Increased alertness  
- Sweating and flushing  
- Temporary pain desensitization with repeated exposure  

Medical capsaicin products take advantage of this desensitization. High-concentration capsaicin patches are used under medical supervision for certain nerve pain conditions, including post-herpetic neuralgia and some neuropathic pain syndromes.

## 4. Skin and Muscles: From Burning to Pain Relief

Capsaicin applied to the skin can initially burn, sting, or redden the area. With repeated or controlled exposure, however, it can reduce the activity of pain-signaling nerves.

Capsaicin creams are used for:

- Arthritis pain  
- Muscle aches  
- Nerve pain  
- Back or joint discomfort  
- Some forms of diabetic neuropathy, under medical guidance  

The effect is not instant. Many topical capsaicin treatments require repeated use over days or weeks. Users must avoid touching the eyes, genitals, or broken skin after applying it, and should wash hands thoroughly.

## 5. Heart and Blood Vessels: Heat, Circulation, and Metabolism

Eating chilies can cause flushing, sweating, and a sense of warmth. Capsaicin may influence blood vessel function, inflammation, and lipid metabolism, though research is still developing.

Some population studies have associated regular chili consumption with lower rates of certain cardiovascular outcomes. However, such studies cannot prove that chilies alone are responsible; people who eat chilies may also differ in diet, lifestyle, genetics, or environment.

Possible cardiovascular-related effects include:

- Temporary increase in heart rate  
- Flushing from blood vessel changes  
- Mild thermogenic effect  
- Potential support for vascular function  

People with heart conditions should be cautious with extreme chili challenges, which can place stress on the body.

## 6. Digestive System: Stimulation and Irritation

Chilies can stimulate saliva and gastric secretions, making food feel more appetizing and aiding digestion for some people. But they can also irritate the digestive tract, especially in high doses.

Possible effects include:

- Increased appetite or digestive stimulation  
- Heartburn or acid reflux  
- Abdominal cramping  
- Diarrhea  
- Burning sensation during bowel movements  

Contrary to an old belief, spicy food does not directly “burn holes” in the stomach. In fact, capsaicin has been studied for effects on stomach lining protection and blood flow. But for people with reflux disease, irritable bowel syndrome, ulcers, gastritis, or sensitive digestion, chilies can worsen symptoms.

## 7. Metabolism and Weight: A Small Thermogenic Push

Capsaicin may slightly increase thermogenesis — the body’s heat production — and may modestly influence appetite. Some studies suggest that spicy foods can increase energy expenditure a little or reduce calorie intake in certain settings.

But chilies are not a weight-loss cure. Any metabolic effect is usually small and depends on dose, tolerance, diet, and individual biology.

Potential metabolic effects include:

- Slight increase in calorie burning  
- Short-term appetite modulation  
- Increased body heat and sweating  
- Possible effects on fat oxidation  

In practical terms, chilies may support a healthy diet by making vegetables, legumes, and lean proteins more flavorful — but they cannot replace overall nutrition and exercise.

## 8. Immune and Inflammatory Responses

Chili peppers contain more than capsaicin. They also provide vitamins, antioxidants, and plant compounds, including:

- Vitamin C  
- Vitamin A precursors such as beta-carotene  
- Flavonoids  
- Phenolic compounds  
- Capsaicinoids  

These compounds may contribute to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Laboratory studies have found antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties in chili extracts, but translating those findings into real-world medical benefits is complex.

Eating chilies as part of a balanced diet may support general health, but they should not be treated as antibiotics or substitutes for medical care.

---

# Medicinal Uses of Chili Compounds

The strongest medical evidence for chili-derived treatment involves pain management, particularly topical capsaicin.

## Capsaicin Is Used For:

- Osteoarthritis discomfort  
- Post-herpetic neuralgia after shingles  
- Certain peripheral nerve pain conditions  
- Muscle and joint pain  
- Some neuropathic pain syndromes  

Researchers have also studied capsaicin for:

- Metabolic health  
- Blood pressure regulation  
- Inflammation  
- Cancer biology in laboratory settings  
- Gut function  
- Itch relief  

However, many of these areas need more clinical evidence. Capsaicin can produce interesting effects in cells and animals, but that does not automatically mean eating very hot peppers will prevent or treat disease.

---

# The Risks: When Heat Becomes Harm

For most healthy adults, moderate chili consumption is safe. The risks rise with very hot peppers, extracts, competitive eating, or direct contact with sensitive tissues.

Possible adverse effects include:

- Severe mouth and throat pain  
- Vomiting  
- Reflux or gastritis flare-ups  
- Diarrhea  
- Dehydration from sweating or vomiting  
- Eye injury from direct contact  
- Skin irritation or burns from concentrated products  
- Breathing difficulty in sensitive individuals  

Extremely hot peppers and capsaicin extracts should be handled carefully. Gloves are recommended when cutting ghost chilies or similarly hot varieties. Children and pets should be kept away from concentrated chili products.

People with gastrointestinal disease, heart disease, pregnancy-related reflux, or medication concerns should seek medical advice if chilies trigger symptoms.

---

# Why Some People Handle Heat Better

Tolerance to chili varies widely. Factors include:

- Genetics  
- Cultural exposure  
- Frequency of chili consumption  
- Nerve receptor sensitivity  
- Gut sensitivity  
- Expectations and learned behavior  

Regular chili eaters often develop greater tolerance, partly because repeated capsaicin exposure can desensitize sensory nerves. That helps explain how someone like Anandita Dutta Tamuly could perform a ghost chili feat that would overwhelm most people. But tolerance is not immunity. Even experienced chili eaters can suffer serious effects from excessive intake.

---

# A Fiery Food With Real Potential

Chili peppers occupy a rare space between food, medicine, and spectacle. They can make a meal vivid, stimulate the senses, and provide compounds with genuine therapeutic value. Capsaicin’s role in pain relief is well established in topical medicine, and ongoing research continues to examine how chilies may affect metabolism, inflammation, circulation, and nerve signaling.

Yet the lesson of the ghost chili is balance. The same pepper that fascinates scientists and chefs can punish the body when treated as a dare. Gordon Ramsay’s encounter with an Indian woman’s ghost chili record attempt captured the drama of human tolerance, but everyday health benefits are more likely to come from regular, moderate use — a little fire in the food, not a medical emergency on a plate.

# What Chilies Do to Your Body

In the northeastern Indian state of Assam, a woman once turned a local staple into an international spectacle: Anandita Dutta Tamuly reportedly ate 51 ghost peppers in two minutes, then rubbed the fiery fruit into her eyes for good measure. The performance, staged in 2009 with celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay looking on, made headlines because the pepper involved was not an ordinary chili. It was the **bhut jolokia**, or **ghost pepper**, then widely described as one of the hottest chilies in the world.

To understand what that means, consider the numbers. Chili heat is measured in **Scoville Heat Units**, or SHU, a scale based on the concentration of capsaicinoids—the chemicals that create the sensation of burning. A typical **jalapeño** ranges from about **2,500 to 8,000 SHU**. **Tabasco sauce** is often in the same general neighborhood, roughly **2,500 to 5,000 SHU**, depending on the product. A **habanero** can reach **100,000 to 350,000 SHU**.

The ghost pepper can exceed **1 million SHU**.

That does not mean it is “hot” in the way a stove is hot. Chilies do not burn tissue by temperature. Instead, they hack the nervous system.

## The chemistry of “heat”

The main compound responsible for chili heat is **capsaicin**, concentrated especially in the white pith and membranes inside the pepper, rather than the seeds themselves. Capsaicin binds to a receptor in the body called **TRPV1**, which normally detects heat and physical abrasion. When capsaicin activates this receptor, the brain interprets the signal as burning—even though no actual thermal burn is occurring.

This is why a chili can make your mouth feel as if it is on fire, your face flush, your nose run, and your scalp sweat. The body reacts as though it needs to cool itself down.

The result can include:

- A burning sensation in the mouth and throat  
- Sweating and flushed skin  
- Watery eyes and runny nose  
- Hiccups or coughing  
- Increased saliva production  
- A temporary rise in heart rate  
- Stomach cramping or intestinal discomfort in sensitive people  

For many chili lovers, the discomfort is part of the appeal. Capsaicin can trigger the release of **endorphins** and **dopamine**, chemicals linked with pleasure, relief and reward. That “chili high” helps explain why people return to spicy foods even after a painful first encounter.

## Why milk helps and water doesn’t

One of the classic mistakes after biting into a very hot pepper is reaching for water. Capsaicin is **fat-soluble**, not water-soluble, so water tends to spread the compound around the mouth rather than wash it away.

Dairy products can work better because milk contains **casein**, a protein that helps loosen capsaicin from nerve receptors. Yogurt, ice cream, or whole milk may be more effective than plain water. Fatty foods can also help dissolve capsaicin. Sugary foods sometimes reduce the perception of heat, though they do not neutralize the compound in the same way.

## A brief history of chilies

Chilies are now central to cuisines across India, Thailand, China, Korea, Ethiopia, Mexico, the Caribbean and beyond, but they originated in the **Americas**. Archaeological evidence suggests people have been cultivating and eating chilies for thousands of years, particularly in regions of present-day Mexico, Central America and South America.

Their global spread came after European contact with the Americas in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Portuguese and Spanish traders carried chilies across oceans, and the plants thrived in warm climates. In India, chilies arrived relatively recently in historical terms, but they became so deeply embedded in regional cooking that many dishes now seem unimaginable without them.

The ghost pepper itself is associated with India’s Northeast, especially Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Locally known by names including **bhut jolokia**, **bih jolokia** and **naga jolokia**, it has been used in chutneys, pickles, curries and even as a folk remedy. Its intense heat also made it useful as an elephant deterrent in some agricultural areas.

## What happens in the digestive system

Once swallowed, capsaicin continues to stimulate nerves along the digestive tract. For most people, moderate amounts of chili are not harmful, though they may be uncomfortable. In some, especially those unaccustomed to spicy foods, capsaicin can cause stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea or a burning sensation during bowel movements.

Contrary to a common belief, spicy food does not directly “burn holes” in the stomach. It does not cause ulcers by itself. Most stomach ulcers are linked to **Helicobacter pylori** infection or long-term use of certain painkillers such as NSAIDs. However, chilies can aggravate symptoms in people who already have gastritis, reflux disease, irritable bowel syndrome or other digestive sensitivities.

Very high doses—such as eating large numbers of superhot peppers—can provoke more serious reactions, including severe vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, or in rare cases medical emergencies. Extreme chili-eating contests have occasionally been linked to esophageal injury, severe headaches or dangerously high stress responses in susceptible individuals.

## Possible health benefits

Despite their fiery reputation, chilies may have benefits when eaten in reasonable amounts as part of a balanced diet.

Research has suggested that capsaicin and chili-rich diets may be associated with:

- Improved circulation and temporary increases in metabolic rate  
- Reduced appetite in some people  
- Anti-inflammatory effects in certain contexts  
- Pain relief when capsaicin is used topically in creams or patches  
- Possible links to lower rates of some cardiovascular risks in population studies  

Topical capsaicin is used medically for conditions such as nerve pain, arthritis pain and post-herpetic neuralgia. In these treatments, repeated exposure reduces the sensitivity of pain-signaling nerves.

However, eating chilies is not a cure-all. Many studies on chili consumption are observational, meaning they can show associations but not prove cause and effect. A person who eats chilies may also have other dietary or lifestyle habits that influence health.

## Can you build tolerance?

Yes. Regular chili eaters often become less sensitive to capsaicin over time. Repeated exposure can desensitize TRPV1 receptors, meaning the same pepper may feel less intense after months or years of spicy eating. Cultural familiarity also matters: people raised with chili-heavy cuisines often learn early how to manage the burn.

But tolerance has limits. A ghost pepper is still a ghost pepper. Even experienced chili eaters can be overwhelmed by superhot varieties, especially when eaten raw or in large quantities.

## The bottom line

Chilies trick the body into sensing heat, setting off a cascade of reactions: sweating, burning, tearing, coughing, pleasure, pain and sometimes gastrointestinal regret. In moderate amounts, they are safe for most people and may offer some health benefits. In extreme amounts—such as eating dozens of ghost peppers—they become a test of physiology as much as appetite.

The woman in Assam who ate 51 ghost peppers was not merely sampling a spicy snack. She was demonstrating an extraordinary tolerance to one of the most potent natural irritants in the culinary world. For the rest of us, the safer lesson is simple: respect the pepper, know your limits, and keep the milk nearby.

# Why Chilies Burn: The Science, History and Health Debate Behind the World’s Hottest Fruit

**By International Health and Science Desk**

From street markets in Mexico City to curry houses in Mumbai, from Sichuan hotpot restaurants to West African stews, chilies are among the world’s most widely used ingredients. They are valued not only for their flavor but for a sensation that is closer to pain than taste: heat.

That heat comes mainly from a group of chemical compounds known as **capsaicinoids**, especially **capsaicin**. These substances have shaped cuisines, trade routes, folk remedies and modern medical research for more than 500 years. Today, scientists are still examining whether chilies can help digestion, immunity, pain control and cardiovascular health — while also warning that too much heat can carry risks.

## The Chemistry of Heat

Chilies are “hot” because capsaicin binds to a receptor in the body called **TRPV1**, short for transient receptor potential vanilloid 1. This receptor is normally activated by high temperatures, acidity and physical irritation. It helps the nervous system detect burning heat and tissue damage.

When capsaicin touches the tongue, throat, stomach lining or skin, it tricks the body into thinking it has encountered heat. The result is a familiar cascade: burning pain, sweating, flushing, watery eyes, runny nose and sometimes hiccups.

Unlike sugar or salt, chili heat is not technically a taste. It is a pain and temperature signal. That explains why chilies can feel hot even on the skin or in the eyes, and why water does little to relieve the burn. Capsaicin is fat-soluble, not water-soluble. Dairy products, oils or starchy foods often work better because they help dissolve or disperse the compound.

The plant’s evolutionary purpose is thought to be defensive. Capsaicin discourages many mammals from eating chili fruits, while birds — which are less sensitive to capsaicin — can eat them and spread the seeds. This helps the plant reproduce.

## How Scoville Units Measure the Burn

The world’s most famous measure of chili heat is the **Scoville Heat Unit**, or **SHU**. It was developed in 1912 by American pharmacist **Wilbur Scoville**, who devised what became known as the **Scoville Organoleptic Test**.

In the original method, chili extract was diluted in sugar water until a panel of tasters could no longer detect heat. The more dilution required, the higher the Scoville rating. For example, if an extract had to be diluted 5,000 times before the heat disappeared, it would be rated at 5,000 SHU.

The scale covers a vast range:

- **Bell pepper:** 0 SHU  
- **Poblano pepper:** roughly 1,000–2,000 SHU  
- **Jalapeño:** about 2,500–8,000 SHU  
- **Cayenne pepper:** about 30,000–50,000 SHU  
- **Habanero:** often 100,000–350,000 SHU  
- **Ghost pepper:** more than 1,000,000 SHU  
- **Carolina Reaper and similar superhots:** often above 1,500,000 SHU  
- **Pure capsaicin:** about 16,000,000 SHU  

Today, laboratories usually measure capsaicinoid concentration using **high-performance liquid chromatography**, or HPLC. This method is more precise than relying on human tasters. The chemical results can then be converted into Scoville Heat Units.

Even so, Scoville ratings can vary widely. Growing conditions, climate, soil, ripeness and plant genetics all influence a chili’s heat. Two peppers of the same variety may not have exactly the same burn.

## From the Americas to the World

Chilies are native to the Americas and were cultivated by Indigenous peoples for thousands of years before European contact. They were used as food, medicine, preservative and ritual substance in different cultures across Central and South America.

After **Christopher Columbus’s voyage in 1492**, chilies became part of the Columbian Exchange, the vast transfer of crops, animals, diseases and goods between the Old and New Worlds. Columbus and other Europeans encountered chilies in the Caribbean and Americas. Because Europeans were searching for black pepper and other valuable spices, they called the fiery fruits “peppers,” a name that remains despite the plants being unrelated to true pepper, *Piper nigrum*.

Portuguese and Spanish traders helped spread chilies rapidly across Africa, Asia and Europe. Within a few generations, they became deeply embedded in cuisines far from their American origins. India, China, Thailand, Korea, Hungary, Ethiopia and many other regions adopted chilies so thoroughly that they now seem ancient to local food traditions.

## A Long Medical History

Chilies were not only culinary goods. They were also incorporated into medicine.

Indigenous American communities used chili preparations for pain, digestive complaints, respiratory symptoms and as topical irritants. After chilies reached Europe, physicians and apothecaries experimented with them as warming agents, stimulants and digestive aids. In the early modern period, chili-based preparations were used to “heat” the body in medical systems influenced by humoral theory, which classified foods and medicines according to qualities such as hot, cold, wet and dry.

By the 19th and 20th centuries, capsaicin and chili extracts appeared in liniments, plasters and ointments for muscle pain, arthritis and neuralgia. Modern medicine still uses capsaicin, particularly in topical creams and high-concentration patches for certain chronic pain conditions.

The scientific understanding has changed dramatically. Instead of simply “warming” the body, capsaicin is now understood to act on nerve receptors, especially TRPV1. Repeated exposure can reduce the amount of certain pain-signaling chemicals, including substance P, and can desensitize local nerves. This helps explain why capsaicin can initially burn but later reduce pain.

## Digestion: Irritant or Aid?

The digestive effects of chilies are complex.

For many people, moderate chili consumption stimulates saliva and gastric secretions, which may support appetite and digestion. Spicy foods can also increase gut motility in some individuals. In traditional medicine systems, chilies have often been used to “wake up” the digestive system.

However, chilies can also cause discomfort. High doses may trigger burning in the mouth, throat, stomach or rectum. People with **irritable bowel syndrome**, functional dyspepsia, acid reflux or inflammatory bowel conditions may find that spicy foods worsen symptoms. Capsaicin can increase sensations of abdominal pain in sensitive individuals because the gut also contains TRPV1 receptors.

Contrary to older beliefs, chilies are not considered a direct cause of stomach ulcers. Most peptic ulcers are linked to **Helicobacter pylori** infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Still, spicy foods can aggravate symptoms in people who already have gastritis, ulcers or reflux.

In short, chilies may aid digestion for some but irritate the digestive tract for others. Tolerance varies greatly by individual, diet and dose.

## Immunity: Vitamins, Antioxidants and Limits

Fresh chilies can be rich in **vitamin C**, **vitamin A precursors**, flavonoids and other antioxidants. These nutrients contribute to normal immune function and help protect cells from oxidative stress.

Capsaicin also has anti-inflammatory effects in some laboratory and animal studies. Researchers have investigated whether chili compounds influence immune signaling, metabolism and gut microbiota. Some findings are promising, but they do not mean chilies are a cure or a substitute for vaccination, balanced nutrition or medical care.

Public health experts caution against exaggerated claims. Eating chilies may be part of a healthy diet, especially when they replace excess salt, sugar or heavy sauces. But the immune system is influenced by many factors, including sleep, age, infections, chronic disease, vaccination status and overall diet.

## Pain: From Fire to Relief

One of the clearest medical uses of capsaicin is pain management.

Topical capsaicin creams and patches are used for conditions such as osteoarthritis pain, post-herpetic neuralgia after shingles, diabetic neuropathy and some other nerve-related pain syndromes. The treatment works by overstimulating pain receptors at first and then reducing their sensitivity over time.

Patients often feel burning, stinging or warmth when treatment begins. With repeated use, the nerves become less reactive. High-dose capsaicin patches are applied under medical supervision because they can cause intense temporary discomfort.

This paradox — a painful substance used to reduce pain — is one reason capsaicin remains of major interest to neuroscientists. It has helped researchers understand how the body senses heat and pain, contributing to discoveries that were recognized with the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on temperature and touch receptors.

Still, capsaicin is not appropriate for everyone. It should not be applied to broken skin, eyes or mucous membranes, and users should wash hands carefully after applying creams. In severe cases, improper exposure can cause significant burning and irritation.

## Cardiovascular Health: Promise and Precaution

Population studies have reported associations between regular chili consumption and lower rates of cardiovascular disease or overall mortality in some groups. Scientists have proposed several possible explanations.

Capsaicin may influence blood vessel function, inflammation, cholesterol metabolism, blood pressure regulation and body weight. Spicy foods may also help reduce salt intake by making food flavorful without as much sodium. Diets rich in vegetables, legumes and spices are often linked with better heart health overall.

But researchers emphasize that association is not proof of causation. People who eat chilies may differ in many ways from those who do not. Their broader diet, income, activity level, smoking habits or access to healthcare may influence outcomes.

For most healthy adults, moderate chili consumption appears safe and may fit well within a heart-healthy diet. But very spicy foods can cause temporary increases in heart rate, sweating and discomfort. People with certain heart conditions, severe reflux or medication sensitivities may need individualized medical advice.

## Risks of Extreme Heat

The global fascination with “superhot” peppers has raised safety concerns. Competitive chili eating and viral challenges involving extremely hot peppers or concentrated extracts can lead to vomiting, severe abdominal pain, fainting and, in rare cases, emergency medical visits.

There have been case reports linking extreme chili exposure to complications such as esophageal injury from forceful vomiting, severe headaches, and reversible narrowing of brain arteries. Such events are uncommon, but they show that concentrated capsaicin is not harmless.

Children are especially vulnerable to accidental exposure. Chili powders, hot sauces and pepper sprays can irritate the eyes and airways. People with asthma or respiratory sensitivity may experience coughing, wheezing or breathing difficulty after inhaling chili particles or aerosols.

Capsaicin supplements also deserve caution. Concentrated capsules can cause stomach upset and may interact with medications or medical conditions. Anyone with chronic digestive disease, pregnancy-related reflux, cardiovascular disease or complex medication use should consult a clinician before taking high-dose chili extracts.

## A Global Ingredient With a Double Edge

Chilies occupy a rare place in human culture: they are food, spice, medicine, irritant and, at times, test of endurance. Their heat is not merely flavor but a chemical alarm signal that humans have learned to enjoy.

The Scoville scale gave the world a language for comparing that fire, while modern chemistry has revealed the molecules behind it. Since Columbus’s voyages helped carry chilies beyond the Americas, they have transformed diets and medical practices across continents.

Their health effects remain a balance of benefit and risk. In moderate amounts, chilies can add nutrients, flavor and possible metabolic or cardiovascular advantages. Capsaicin has proven value in some pain treatments. But for sensitive individuals, and especially at extreme doses, chilies can irritate the digestive tract, skin, eyes and airways.

For most people, the advice from nutrition and medical experts is straightforward: enjoy the heat if you tolerate it, avoid extremes, and treat chilies as one part of a varied diet — not as a miracle cure.
